catalog_quote: In Khowar, word stress is lexically determined; that is, in each word a specific syllable is stressed. Stress has several functions in Khowar. First, it is lexically contrastive, indicating a meaning difference in several pairs of basic underived words; see examples in Table 2.10. Stress plays a morphological role in several contexts, for example in deriving nouns from adjectives, as in iskúrdi ‘short’ → iskurdí ‘shortness’. [...] Disyllabic nouns are stressed either on their final syllable: apák ‘mouth’, arqá ‘back’; or on their initial (in this case penultimate) syllable: áɫi ‘duck’, náqul ‘proverb’, ʋrázun ‘wing’. Trisyllabic nouns can be stressed either on the penultimate syllable, as in išnári ‘thing’, iskúrdi ‘short’, or on the final syllable, for example, adiná ‘Friday’, panǰaráṣ ‘full moon’, iskurdí ‘shortness’. [...] Morphological processes, either derivational, as in iskúrdi ‘short’ → iskurdí ‘shortness’ (see also Chapter 3), or inflectional, as in c̣hétur ‘field.dir’ → c̣hetr-ó ‘field-obl’, c̣hétr-o ‘field-loc4’, result in stress shift and morphophonological changes. [...] Sentence stress is to be distinguished from lexical stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically assigned and contrastive (káɫi 'noodle soup' vs kaɫí 'yoke stick', béɫu 'basket' vs beɫú 'flute'); in uninflected words it falls on the final or the penultimate syllable (Liljegren & Khan 2017: final is the most frequent pattern, antepenult marginal at best). Certain suffixes are inherently stressed (oblique -ó, obl.pl -án, infinitive -ík, nominaliser -í, plural -gíni) and take the main stress when added (dust > dustó, iskúrdi > iskurdí), i.e. main stress goes to the rightmost lexically stressed morpheme; but stems with the lexical low-rising tone (lengthened vowel, e.g. doón 'ghee', braár 'brother') and a small set of kin terms (nan, tat, beč, mik) keep stress on the stem before -o/-an, and disyllables with final stress keep it (šapír-o). A marginal lexical low-rising tone (with vowel elongation) contrasts with default high-falling pitch on a small number of words (don 'tooth' vs doón 'ghee').
new_statements.secondary_stress: In compounds the primary stress of the first element is demoted to secondary stress (bašar̩.dóyu 'member of a funeral procession'); when a stressed suffix attaches to a polysyllable the earlier stress becomes secondary (noʋes-gíni). Strand 2012 likewise describes a secondary accent level in compounds/multi-word sequences on the normally accented vowel of a constituent. No rhythmic secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: Low-tone (lengthened) monosyllabic stems and kin terms nan/tat/beč/mik/lu retain stem stress before oblique -o (nán-o, brár-o) whereas most monosyllables shift (dust-ó, šam-ó); žaʋ, ʋaʋ shift (žaʋ-ó); lu 'word' > lú-o is called an unexplained puzzle; enclitics like di 'also' unstressed; perfective participle stress placement varies; sentence/emphatic stress can override (γoš no boy-án).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical word stress in citation and inflected word forms; Bashir explicitly separates sentence stress (emphasis/focus shifts, utterance-final lengthening) from lexical stress. Description based on conservative Upper Chitral varieties (fieldwork 1986-2010); Liljegren & Khan's corroborating JIPA account is of Mastuj (Upper Chitral) speech, with acoustic note that pitch height/change is the main correlate of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe Upper Chitral Khowar: Bashir 2025 is based on fieldwork (1986-2010) with speakers of the conservative Upper Chitral varieties (Mulkhow/Torkhow/Mastuj area), Liljegren & Khan 2017 on the speech of Mastuj; both are Khowar proper = khow1242 (ISO khw). Bashir notes only minor dialect variation (Chitral Town, Swat Ushu/Mataltal, Ghizer/Gupis-Yasin in Gilgit-Baltistan); no separate glottocodes involved.

tone_statements.quote: The normal unaccented phonation of vowels in Khow`ar is produced with anterior phonation and a concomitant front tensing of the larynx. [...] Accented phonation is produced with either tight anterior phonation or posterior phonation, concomitant with the oral articulation of a vowel. There are two levels of accent, primary and secondary, above the level of default phonation. The default accentual level is primary. Primary accented phonation is indicated by an accent mark (` for anterior phonation or ´ for posterior phonation) written before the accented vowel. [...] The position of accent within words is distinctive. Accented phonation may occur on the penultimate or the final syllable in a simple, non-compounded word, as in the word-pair b`eḷu ‘straw bucket’ vs. beḷ`u ‘pipe; flute’. A secondary level of accent appears in multi-word sequences. Secondary accent may be produced by either anterior or posterior phonation. [...] Compared to the normal, primary accent described above, the pitch of secondary accent is not as high for anterior phonation and not as low for posterior phonation. In compound words secondary accent falls on the normally accented vowel of a constituent word.
tone_statements.locator: §3.2.1 'Khow`ar; Default Anterior Phonation, Anterior or Posterior Accent without Position; Tones', printed p. 23, incl; Table 29; secondary accent also §2.2.2…

tone_statements.summary: Confirms the catalog's lexical kind and restricted-tone class: accent position is distinctive (minimal pair b`eḷu vs beḷ`u) and the accented vowel carries a two-way contrast, anterior accent (raised pitch, written `) vs posterior accent (lowered pitch, written ´), e.g. g`oḷ 'throat' vs g´oḷ 'gully' (Table 29, p. 23); §2.2.2 p. 4: 'a raised pitch for accented anterior phonation and a lowered pitch

sources.note: 'Stress, tone and vowel duration' (pp. 224-227): 'The placement of stress is lexically contrastive in Khowar. The most frequent stress pattern is one with main stress on the final syllable, but it may also fall on the penultimate (and possibly even the antepenultimate) syllable of an uninflected word'; main correlate pitch, often with intensity; a minority of affixes lexically stressed, main stress on the rightmost lexically stressed syllable; separate lexical low(-rising) tone on some items which retains stress under affixation. Speech of Mastuj, Upper Chitral.

tone.quote: Характерна оппозиция w — у; фонема r представлена звукотипом # перед смычными глухими. Ударение тяготеет к исходу слова. Наблюдаются тоновые оппозиции (появляющиеся исторически при уграте древними звонкими придыхательными элемента аспирации). 51.1. Структура слога не изучена. 5.1.2. Типы чередований не изучены.
tone.translation: The opposition w — y is characteristic; the phoneme r is represented by the sound type [#] before voiceless stops. Stress gravitates toward the end of the word. Tonal oppositions are observed (arising historically when the old voiced aspirates lost the element of aspiration). 5.1.1. Syllable structure has not been studied. 5.1.2. Types of alternations have not been studied.
